source.title: Negative Pre-activations Differentiate Syntax
source.authors: Linghao Kong; Angelina Ning; Micah Adler; N. Shavit

record.tranche_reason: The study refines the interpretation of selected language-model neurons: its token-pair analyses report coherent syntactic distinctions, but it does not test how common polysemanticity is or whether canonical polysemantic neurons have one shared feature.
record.gate_note: The study's main experiments causally test the syntax function of negative pre-activations, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The detailed token-pair analyses bear narrowly on V6 by reporting syntactic patterns for selected Wasserstein neurons. Its causal ablations, benchmark scores, and layerwise results are not rows here because they do not measure whether a neuron's differentiated inputs form a coherent feature.
record.test_reason: The study does not measure whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. Its token-pair analysis looks at Wasserstein neurons that map similar inputs to distant outputs. The paper calls this an entanglement complementary to superposition, not polysemanticity. Neurons were selected by Wasserstein distance or mapping difficulty, not as known polysemantic neurons, so no row bears on any version. Polysemanticity and superposition appear only in the related-work discussion.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it understates the main claim. The authors conclude that negative pre-activations in a sparse set of Wasserstein neurons are a functional substrate for syntax. Sign-specific ablations of about 1% of neurons sharply harm BLiMP and TSE, while perplexity-matched ablations of low-WD neurons harm non-grammatical tasks more (a double dissociation). The token-pair analyses are illustrative; the authors make no claim about how common polysemanticity is.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Wasserstein/mapping-difficulty selection, token-pair analysis, and sign-specific interventions on language-model MLP neurons; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analysis or a SoLU comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported negative-negative pair pattern differs between Pythia 1.4B and Llama 3.1 8B: Pythia shows high prevalence in early layers, while Llama has a lower overall rate with positive-negative pairs dominating across depth. The pair-selection procedure also differs between these analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia 1.4B, the token pairs that high-WD/MD neurons separate most are enriched for function-word POS classes (determiners, adpositions, punctuation, numerals). Often both outputs of a pair are negative (8 of 10 pairs for neuron 5176).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Entangled (high-Wasserstein-distance) neurons in smooth-activation LMs separate similar inputs along syntactic categories, mainly through negative pre-activations.

record.problems: The interpretability evidence is qualitative and focuses on selected Wasserstein neurons and their most differentiated pairs, rather than a representative sample of neurons. Detailed neuron examples are from Pythia 1.4B; the study does not quantify how many neurons have coherent versus unrelated mixtures or test canonical polysemantic neurons.
record.rows_left_out: The main negative-preactivation ablations, grammar benchmark results, and layerwise syntax effects are omitted because they measure causal effects on grammatical performance rather than whether neuron inputs form a coherent feature. The layerwise negative-negative pair proportions and training trends are also omitted because they characterize sign patterns, not polysemanticity or shared feature meaning.

untested.parts: All; no share of polysemantic MLP neurons by layer.
All. The ReLU vs GELU comparison (Fig. 1) concerns pre-activation distribution shape, not a polysemantic share.
All; no canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined.
The paper argues negative pre-activations carry signal, but does not test whether polysemanticity judgments change with the activation range examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/V6 assignment conflates input differentiation of similar inputs with polysemanticity. The paper explicitly frames Wasserstein-neuron entanglement as distinct from the superposition sense in which neurons share multiple features. The interpretability-of-negative-region argument is loosely related to V7 but makes no polysemanticity judgment.

versions.untested_parts: The share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how that share varies by language-model layer.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure, including effects of initialization, regularization, or training noise.
The share of polysemantic neurons under different activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and whether it can be lowered without a large performance loss.

The study examines selected Wasserstein neurons, not canonical polysemantic neurons such as the cited vision example. It does not estimate how common truly unrelated mixtures are or establish that most neurons have one coherent job.
Whether polysemanticity judgments change when different activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods are used.

rows.subject: Pythia 1.4B, neuron 5176
rows.operation_detail: Selected and inspected the ten token pairs with the greatest normalized output-distance to input-distance ratio.
rows.measure: Qualitative token/POS patterns among the most differentiated pairs; sign pattern of pair outputs.
rows.value: The pairs were described as overwhelmingly grammatical; 8 of the 10 had both pre-activation outputs negative. An example distinguished a preposition from a determiner.
rows.note: The authors interpret the examples as syntactic functional-word distinctions. The selected pairs are not a general sample of the neuron's responses.
rows.check: Measures which similar-input token pairs neuron 5176 separates most (top 10 of 1,000 random pairs). This is differentiation, not a response to unrelated features. The neuron was not identified as canonically polysemantic, so the row cannot bear on V6.

conditions.value: top output pairs by distance relative to input distance

rows.value: The neuron strongly separated the token 'and' from a variety of other tokens.
rows.note: The reported distinction is centered on a conjunction, but the paper does not characterize the other tokens as one coherent category.
rows.check: Qualitative token-separation pattern of a WD-selected neuron. It does not measure polysemantic responding or reinterpret a known polysemantic neuron.

rows.subject: Pythia 1.4B, additional neurons in the second up projection layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared POS categories in the top differentiated token pairs with their base rates in WikiText 2.

conditions.value: additional neurons in the second up projection layer

rows.baseline: POS base rates in the full WikiText 2 dataset
rows.value: Determiners, adpositions, punctuation, numerals, and verbs were described as heavily enriched among differentiated tokens; no numerical enrichment values are stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors say the patterns suggest many neurons implement relatively coherent, fine-grained syntactic distinctions; they do not give a prevalence estimate.
rows.check: POS enrichment among the most differentiated pairs, compared with WikiText 2 base rates, for WD-selected neurons. No enrichment numbers are given in the text, and it says nothing about whether these neurons respond to unrelated features.
